newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr a victim of diminishing returns.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr a victim of diminishing returns.

text.p: The Australian dollar was under a cloud in late trade Tuesday as the market struggled to come to terms with its vanishing yield advantage.

Dealers said the currency had leant on US$0.7650 support through a thin session with exporter and options-related bids soaking up early U.S. fund offers. But many suspected investors in London and New York, refreshed by a long weekend, would be ready to resume the selling seen after Friday's rate cut.
Today's domestic data on business investment were stronger than expected for the first quarter, but showed some worrying slippage in forward spending estimates for 1997/98.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar was languishing at US$0.7650/55 having ventured as high as US$0.7675 resistance this morning after bouncing from a US$0.7635 low offshore.
That was a shade down on Monday's late US$0.7662/67 and far below the US$0.7770 level held ahead of Friday's surprise rate cut from the Reserve Bank.

Chart watchers said there was a still a chance of a short covering rise to the US$0.7710/20 area which marked the floor of the dollar's range for six weeks before Friday's 1-1/2 cent dive. But most recommended selling at those levels if seen for an eventual re-test of US$0.7635 and retracement to US$0.7550.
On the crosses the currency trailed off to 88.79/89 yen from an early 89.46 high, but was steady on Monday's late 88.80/90.
The yen found support from rising Japanese bond yields as heavy options-related selling saw the 10-year JGB benchmark jump to a 1997 high of 2.680 percent from a previous 2.580.

That helped the yen recoup some ground from the mark, which itself had benefited from safe haven flows Monday following the surprising strength of the left wing parties in the first round of the French general election.
The local dollar was little more than a spectator to all this and vulnerable to the vagaries of US$/yen.
The U.S. dollar was hovering around 116.00 yen inlate trade having finished Friday at 115.60/70 in New York.
In trade weighted terms the local dollar firmed slightly to 58.3 from a previous 58.0 close, but again was well short of the 59.1 level held before Friday's rate cut.
Analysts said the RBA's generosity with rates had dulled the appetite for this week's helping of domestic economic data.

Which was why a 6.5 percent rise in private capital expenditure for the March quarter had scant market impact even though it easily beat forecasts of a 3.5 percent gain and more than compensated for a 1.6 percent drop in Q4.
The jump in spending promised to contribute a little more to GDP growth in the quarter than previously thought and had some analysts nudging up their forecasts for GDP-A.
However, the RBA's readiness to go for growth meant it might yet ease again if the economy fell short of expectations, and in this regard the CAPEX data actually sounded a warning note.

This came from a survey of investment intentions which showed growth in spending expectations was not nearly as strong as this time last year. The second estimate for 1997/98 spending was up only 1.5 percent on the second estimate for 1996/97 whereas the latter had been 22.7 percent up on that in 1995/96.
Analysts said the slippage in the spending outlook meant the government's budget forecast of eight percent growth in 1997/98 business investment looked in doubt.
However, they emphasised these were very early days and it could be that last week's rate cut would prove timely if it bolstered business investment plans for the year ahead.
Also out this week are figures on business inventories and the balance of payments for Q1, and data on retail trade, the goods and services trade balance and motor vehicle registrations for April.
